newsitem.title: CANADA: France's Tapie defends role in new Lelouch film.
newsitem.headline: France's Tapie defends role in new Lelouch film.

text.p: Disgraced former French businessman, soccer mogul and politician Bernard Tapie on Tuesday defended his role in the latest film by director Claude Lelouch.

Speaking at a news conference marking the North American launch of Lelouch's 35th feature film, "Hommes, femmes, mode d'emploi," ("Men, Women: Instructions for Use,") Tapie said no one had the right to prevent him from making films.
Tapie, 53, who was forced to resign from France's National Assembly last month and faces prison terms for tax fraud and rigging a soccer match, blasted those he called "moralists."
"The day when the law says that someone who is pursued by the courts for a rigged soccer match does not have the right to make films, I will not make films," he said.
"It is not for you, nor for someone else, nor I don't know whom to decide that it is not moral to make films ... because I am reproached for this and that," Tapie said.

In the film Tapie plays a morally dubious lawyer. The film initially attracted large audiences in France but Lelouch said ticket sales were hurt by a boycott by certain members of the public and the media appalled by Tapie's participation.
Lelouch said he noticed Tapie about 25 years ago and was impressed by his ability to communicate with the public. He said he approched him a number of times to act in a film.
He spoke glowingly of Tapie's energy and enthusiasm, saying, "A good actor is someone who tries to make you accept a truth that is his, even if it is not the truth."

Lelouch said that enlisting Tapie as an actor was not a publicity stunt designed to create a box-office rush for tickets. Immediately after Lelouch announced that he would make the film people sent him letters saying they would boycott the film, he said.
